result: In aged mice (8-10 months), c-Jun protein levels in the distal nerve stump 4 days after transection were ~50% lower than in young mice (6-8 weeks). In c-Jun OE/+ mice, this age-dependent decline was prevented, restoring c-Jun levels to those seen in young WT mice, as demonstrated by western blot, qPCR, and immunofluorescence.
evaluation: Claims C39-C44 are directly supported by multiple complementary experimental approaches (western blot, qPCR, immunofluorescence) shown in Figure 1A-C. The data consistently demonstrate reduced c-Jun in aged WT mice and restoration in c-Jun OE/+ mice, with appropriate quantification and statistical analysis.

result: The number of neurons regenerating through the distal stump of aged WT mice was reduced by about 50% compared to young mice. In aged c-Jun OE/+ mice, regeneration of both DRG and motor neurons was restored to levels similar to those in young WT nerves, as measured by neuron back-filling and CGRP+ fiber counts.
evaluation: Claims C45-C48 are well-supported by neuron back-filling experiments (Figure 1D-E) and axon counts (Figure 1F), which provide direct quantitative measures of regeneration. The restoration of regeneration in c-Jun OE/+ mice to young WT levels establishes the functional significance of c-Jun restoration during aging.

result: A mouse model of chronic denervation was established showing that mRNA levels for repair-associated genes (S100b, Ngfr, Gdnf, Shh) and p75NTR protein declined substantially between 1 and 10 weeks of denervation. The capacity of the distal stump to support regeneration declined correspondingly, with only about half as many motor neurons regenerating through 10-week denervated stumps compared to acutely transected stumps.
evaluation: Claims C49-C53 are supported by RNA sequencing (Figure 2A), western blot (Figure 2B), neuron back-filling (Figure 2C), and axon counts (Figure 2D). The multiple complementary approaches establish a robust mouse model of chronic denervation that recapitulates findings from rat studies.

result: c-Jun protein levels in distal stumps showed strong elevation 3 days and 1 week after sciatic nerve cut, followed by a decline to ~40% of 1-week levels at 10 weeks. This decline was confirmed to be Schwann cell-specific using c-Jun cKO mice and was recapitulated in purified Schwann cell cultures in vitro, suggesting the decline is not driven by endoneurial signals.
evaluation: Claims C54-C60 are supported by western blot (Figure 3A-B, D), immunofluorescence (Figure 3C), and qPCR (Figure 3E) data from both in vivo and in vitro experiments. The use of c-Jun cKO mice to verify Schwann cell specificity and the in vitro recapitulation strengthen the conclusion that c-Jun decline is cell-autonomous.

result: At 1 and 3 weeks after denervation, c-Jun protein levels were similar in WT and c-Jun OE/+ mice, both showing ~80-100 fold elevation. However, at 10 weeks, c-Jun declined in WT mice but was maintained in c-Jun OE/+ mice at levels similar to 1 week, as demonstrated by western blot and immunofluorescence.
evaluation: Claims C61-C65 are directly supported by western blot (Figure 4A) and immunofluorescence (Figure 4B) data showing differential c-Jun maintenance between genotypes during chronic denervation. The data establish that c-Jun OE/+ mice can maintain high c-Jun levels that naturally decline in WT mice.

result: In WT mice, the number of DRG and motor neurons regenerating through 10-week denervated nerves was reduced by about 50% compared to acutely cut nerves. In c-Jun OE/+ mice, this decline was prevented, with regeneration through 10-week denervated nerves maintained at levels similar to acutely cut WT nerves, as measured by neuron back-filling and neurofilament+ axon counts.
evaluation: Claims C66-C70, C77 are strongly supported by neuron back-filling experiments (Figure 5A-B) and axon counts (Figure 5C) demonstrating that maintaining c-Jun levels during chronic denervation prevents regeneration failure. This establishes the functional significance of c-Jun maintenance during chronic denervation.

result: Control experiments demonstrated that the regeneration support provided by WT and c-Jun OE/+ nerves was similar early after injury. The number of back-filled neurons in c-Jun OE/+ mice was similar to WT when tracer was applied immediately after transection or 2 weeks after immediate repair, and after nerve crush.
evaluation: Claims C71-C74 are supported by neuron back-filling experiments (Figure 5D-G) that serve as important controls demonstrating that c-Jun OE/+ mice do not have enhanced regeneration under normal conditions, only when c-Jun would otherwise decline (aging or chronic denervation). This strengthens the specificity of the main findings.

result: Under the conditions prevailing in the distal stump of cut nerves, Schwann cells are unable to maintain high c-Jun levels in the long term, and the gradual reduction in c-Jun leads to deterioration of repair cell function, causing regeneration failure.
evaluation: Claims C75-C76 are conclusions drawn from the experimental data on chronic denervation (Figures 3-5). The inference is well-supported by the temporal correlation between c-Jun decline and regeneration failure, and the restoration of both by genetic manipulation.

result: In experiments comparing young and aging animals, Schwann cell and macrophage numbers and density were similar irrespective of genotype or age. There was some decrease in fibroblast density in aged mice, but density and numbers were similar irrespective of genotype. These findings indicate that altered cell numbers are not a significant reason for improved regeneration in aged c-Jun OE/+ nerves.
evaluation: Claims C78-C80, C90 are supported by electron microscopy cell counts (Figure 6A-F). The data effectively rule out differential cell numbers as the primary mechanism for improved regeneration in aged c-Jun OE/+ mice, strengthening the conclusion that c-Jun's effects are primarily functional rather than proliferative.

result: During chronic denervation, Schwann cell numbers declined by ~30% in WT nerves but this decline was prevented in c-Jun OE/+ nerves. Macrophage numbers declined irrespective of genotype. Fibroblast density was elevated in 10-week WT stumps but not in c-Jun OE/+ stumps. However, even in 10-week WT stumps, Schwann cell numbers remained well above those in uninjured nerves.
evaluation: Claims C81-C89, C91-C92 are supported by electron microscopy cell counts (Figure 6G-L). The data show that c-Jun OE/+ prevents some Schwann cell loss during chronic denervation, but the authors appropriately note that cell numbers remain elevated even in WT, suggesting functional changes are more important than cell number changes.

result: In Shh cKO mice, c-Jun protein and phosphorylated c-Jun were decreased in the distal stump 7 days after injury, as was p75NTR. Shh agonists (SAG and purmorphamine) upregulated c-Jun in cultured Schwann cells, while the Shh antagonist cyclopamine downregulated c-Jun and suppressed c-Jun phosphorylation. These findings implicate Shh in promoting Schwann cell c-Jun expression and support an autocrine Shh signaling loop.
evaluation: Claims C94-C96, C99-C101 are supported by western blot data from Shh cKO mice (Figure 7A-C) and cultured Schwann cells treated with Shh agonists/antagonists (Figures 7D-E, 8D). The bidirectional effects (loss-of-function and gain-of-function) provide strong evidence for Shh regulation of c-Jun, though the autocrine loop inference requires additional validation.

result: SAG promoted the elongated bi- or tri-polar shape in vitro that reflects the elongation and branching of repair cells in vivo.
evaluation: Claim C98 is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 8C with quantification of cell area, roundness, and length/√area ratio. The data demonstrate that Shh signaling affects Schwann cell morphology in a manner consistent with repair cell characteristics.

result: RNA sequencing analysis revealed that in uninjured nerves, 1477 genes were differentially expressed between young and aged mice, and in 3-day cut nerves, 398 genes were differentially expressed. The 138 previously identified c-Jun-regulated injury genes showed strong enrichment among age-regulated genes in all comparisons, suggesting the c-Jun-regulated repair program is disproportionately vulnerable during aging.
evaluation: Claims C102-C105, C108-C111 are supported by RNA sequencing data and over-representation analysis (Figure 9A). The enrichment of c-Jun-regulated genes among age-affected genes provides molecular evidence linking c-Jun decline to aging-related regeneration failure, though the inference about vulnerability is interpretive.

result: Trophic factors such as GDNF, BDNF, NGF, erythropoietin, and FGF were not among the differentially expressed genes between young and aged 3-day cut nerves, suggesting that expression of these trophic factors may not explain different regeneration between young and aged mice.
evaluation: Claims C106-C107 are supported by RNA sequencing data analysis and are consistent with previous work (Painter et al., 2014). This negative finding is important as it suggests c-Jun's effects are not mediated through these classical trophic factors, though the inference is somewhat speculative.

result: Gene ontology analysis showed that in aged uninjured WT nerves, downregulated genes were involved in lipid metabolism and myelination, while immune genes were upregulated. In the injury response, aged WT nerves showed reduced activation of immune genes, suppressed MAPK pathways, and enhanced lipid metabolism and Schwann cell differentiation genes, indicating suppressed Schwann cell reprogramming and repair cell activation.
evaluation: Claims C112-C116 are supported by GO analysis (Figure 9B-E) and are consistent with previous literature. The data provide molecular insights into the aging-related changes in Schwann cells, though the inference about suppressed reprogramming is interpretive rather than directly demonstrated.

result: In aged c-Jun OE/+ nerves, pathways associated with protein processing and maturation were upregulated compared to aged WT nerves. Among c-Jun-regulated genes, four genes (Aqp5, Gpr37L1, Igfbp2, Olig1) showed expression defects in aged WT nerves that were restored in aged c-Jun OE/+ nerves where regeneration is restored.
evaluation: Claims C117-C121 are supported by GO analysis (Figure 9F) and RNA sequencing data (Figure 9G-H). The identification of candidate genes whose expression correlates with both c-Jun levels and regeneration provides potential mechanistic insights, though causality is not established.

result: During chronic denervation, expression of 1581 genes changed significantly, with 601 downregulated (including Gdnf, Shh, Ngfr) and 980 upregulated. The 138 c-Jun-regulated genes showed 5.8-fold enrichment among these genes. GO analysis revealed downregulation of cell cycle, DNA replication, glial differentiation, and MAPK pathways, and upregulation of neuro-glia signaling, Notch, and cAMP signaling genes.
evaluation: Claims C122-C127 are supported by RNA sequencing data and GO analysis (Figure 10A-B, Figure 10—figure supplement 1). The data provide comprehensive molecular characterization of chronic denervation and demonstrate that c-Jun-regulated genes are disproportionately affected.

result: In chronically denervated c-Jun OE/+ mice, pathways involved in PNS and Schwann cell development and differentiation were strongly upregulated. Among c-Jun-regulated genes, five genes (Cxcl5, Egfl8, Gas213, Megf10, Pcdh20) showed expression changes during chronic denervation in WT nerves that were restored in c-Jun OE/+ nerves.
evaluation: Claims C128-C131 are supported by GO analysis (Figure 10C) and RNA sequencing data (Figure 10D-E). The identification of candidate genes provides potential mechanistic insights into how c-Jun maintenance preserves regenerative capacity during chronic denervation, though causality is not established.

result: The study concludes that reduced expression of c-Jun is an important factor in repair cell failures during both aging and chronic denervation. In both situations, Schwann cells fail to achieve or maintain high c-Jun levels, and correction of c-Jun expression restores regeneration deficits, providing a common molecular link between these two problems and suggesting manipulation of c-Jun-regulated pathways as a potential therapeutic route.
evaluation: Claims C132-C136 represent the main conclusions of the study, which are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental data demonstrating c-Jun decline in both aging and chronic denervation, and functional restoration of regeneration by genetic c-Jun restoration. The therapeutic speculation (C136) is appropriately cautious.

result: The manuscript provides extensive background on nerve regeneration, repair Schwann cells, the effects of aging and chronic denervation on regeneration, and the role of c-Jun in Schwann cell reprogramming. This background establishes the rationale for investigating c-Jun as a common mechanism underlying regeneration failure in aging and chronic denervation.
evaluation: Claims C1, C10-C38, C93 represent background knowledge and literature review that is well-supported by numerous citations to previous work. These claims establish the scientific context and rationale for the current study but do not represent new findings.
